kwakwakawakw_umelth.name: steal and release the sun, moon, and daylight from their hoarders
kwakwakawakw_umelth.notes: As the transformer Raven (U'meł) he disguises himself, is swallowed and reborn from the daughter of the chief who hoards the celestial lights, then breaks open the boxes to give the world the sun, moon, and stars.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Tales / The Religion of the Kwakiutl Indians

kwakwakawakw_umelth.name: release the salmon and set the rhythm of the tides
kwakwakawakw_umelth.notes: Raven frees the impounded waters and fish and orders the ebb and flow of the sea, a transformer's gift to humankind.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Tales

kwakwakawakw_umelth.name: change his shape to deceive and to transform the primordial world
kwakwakawakw_umelth.notes: The Raven-transformer takes the form of a pine needle, a man, or other beings to work his ends and to fix the present order of the world.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Tales

lakota_wi.name: give light, warmth, and generative power to the world
lakota_wi.notes: As the fourth Superior God and chief among them, Wí is the source of daylight and heat and the quickening power of life.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wi.name: patronize the four cardinal virtues of bravery, fortitude, generosity, and wisdom
lakota_wi.notes: Wí is the patron of the virtues a man must show, and the giver of the rites by which they are demonstrated.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, The Sun Dance and Other Ceremonies of the Oglala Division of the Teton Dakota

lakota_skan.name: impart motion, energy, and spirit to every being
lakota_skan.notes: Škáŋ (Tákuškaŋškaŋ, 'that which moves') is the sky and the source of all movement, who gives to each living thing its niya (breath) and naǧí (spirit).

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_skan.name: judge among the gods and decree the order of the cosmos
lakota_skan.notes: In Walker's accounts Škáŋ is the great arbiter who settles the quarrels of the gods, sentences the offenders at the Feast of the Gods, and ordains the alternation of day and night.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_inyan.name: create the world by opening his veins in self-sacrifice
lakota_inyan.notes: Alone in the original darkness and holding all power in his blue blood, Íŋyaŋ bled himself to form Maká the Earth and the waters, shrinking and hardening into the rock and stone of the world.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_inyan.name: give the waters their being from his blue blood
lakota_inyan.notes: The blood that flowed from him became the waters of the world, and the blue of the sky was the spirit Škáŋ released from it.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Myth

lakota_maka.name: bear and nourish all living things as the ground of the world
lakota_maka.notes: Drawn from Íŋyaŋ's own substance, Maká is the soil and land from which all life springs and to which it returns.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_hanwi.name: rule the night and give it light as the Night-Sun
lakota_hanwi.notes: After her separation from Wí, Škáŋ gave Haŋwí the night to govern; she travels the sky alone by night as the Sun travels by day.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_hanwi.name: wax and wane by covering and uncovering her face in shame
lakota_hanwi.notes: Shamed when the two-faced Ité usurped her seat at the Feast of the Gods, she hides her face, and her covering and uncovering explains the phases of the moon.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_iktomi.name: invent language, names, stories, and games
lakota_iktomi.notes: As Ksá, the first god of wisdom, he devised speech, the names of things, the telling of tales, and the games of the people before his demotion to trickster.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_iktomi.name: scheme, deceive, and change his shape, often to his own ruin
lakota_iktomi.notes: As Iktómi the Spider he is endlessly cunning, able to take many forms, yet is regularly entrapped by his own tricks; he engineered the deception that parted the Sun and the Moon.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Myth

lakota_wakinyan.name: make thunder with his wing-beats and lightning with his glance
lakota_wakinyan.notes: The Winged One of the West produces the thunder by beating his wings and the lightning by the flashing of his eyes.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wakinyan.name: hunt and strike the water monsters with his bolts
lakota_wakinyan.notes: Wakíŋyaŋ is the perpetual enemy of Uŋktéhi and the underwater powers, killing them with lightning — the axis of sky against water in Lakota cosmology.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wakinyan.name: empower the contrary heyókȟa through visions
lakota_wakinyan.notes: Those who dream of the Thunder-beings must become heyókȟa, the sacred clowns who act in reverse; Wakíŋyaŋ's own contrary nature is the source of their power.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_unktehi.name: raise floods and drag down the drowned
lakota_unktehi.notes: Chief of the underwater powers, Uŋktéhi brings the great floods and the deaths by drowning; in one tradition her flood drowned the ancient people.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_unktehi.name: wage perpetual war on the Thunderbird
lakota_unktehi.notes: The horned water-monster is the fixed adversary of Wakíŋyaŋ, the two locked in the battle of water against sky.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wohpe.name: reconcile and harmonize the oppositions among gods and beings
lakota_wohpe.notes: The Mediator and Beautiful One, daughter of Škáŋ, smooths the quarrels of the powers; in the wind cycle she dwelt in Tȟaté's lodge and reared the Whirlwind.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wohpe.name: bring the Sacred Pipe and the seven rites to the people
lakota_wohpe.notes: Identified with White Buffalo Calf Woman (Ptesáŋ Wíŋ), she brought the Lakota the Calf Pipe and taught the Seven Sacred Rites before departing as a buffalo.

sources.reference: Joseph Epes Brown, The Sacred Pipe: Black Elk's Account of the Seven Rites of the Oglala Sioux

lakota_anog_ite.name: teach women the dyeing of porcupine quills and the art of quillwork
lakota_anog_ite.notes: As Double Woman she appears to women in dreams and bestows the craft of quillwork, the origin of the practice among the Lakota.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_anog_ite.name: tempt men with her beautiful face and bring sorrow to the unwary
lakota_anog_ite.notes: Showing only her fair side she lures men; turning, she reveals the second, hideous face. Separated from her children, she is blamed for the pains of childbirth and the crying of infants.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Myth

lakota_tate.name: act as the companion and agent of Škáŋ at the center of the world
lakota_tate.notes: Created by Škáŋ to do his will, Tȟaté the Wind keeps the lodge at the center from which his sons are sent to the quarters.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_tate.name: father and dispatch the Four Winds to the cardinal directions
lakota_tate.notes: By Ité he fathered the Four Winds (Tȟaté Tób) and the late-born Whirlwind, sending each to govern its quarter of the world.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wazi.name: work magic and sorcery as the Old Man wizard
lakota_wazi.notes: Wazí, chief of the underworld people, is a wielder of magic; for abetting Iktómi at the Feast of the Gods he was condemned by Škáŋ to wander the world.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_wakanka.name: see and foretell as the Old Woman seer and witch
lakota_wakanka.notes: Wakáŋka (Kȟaŋká) is a seer of hidden things; condemned for the deception at the Feast of the Gods, she must use her gifts to help the young.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_yumni.name: preside over play, games, courtship, and love
lakota_yumni.notes: The late-born Whirlwind, reared in part by Wóȟpe, became the patron of sport, gambling games, and the games of love and courtship.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_eya.name: govern the West, the close of day and year, and the realm of the Thunder-beings
lakota_eya.notes: Second-born of the Four Winds but holder of the eldest's birthright, Eyá rules the western quarter where the Thunder-beings dwell.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_okaga.name: rule the warm South and bring growth, plenty, and ripening
lakota_okaga.notes: Last-born of the Four Winds, Okáǧa governs the fertile southern quarter of warmth and abundance, set against the cold North.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_yata.name: rule the cold North, the quarter of winter and hardship
lakota_yata.notes: Firstborn of the Four Winds but stripped of the eldest's birthright, Yatá governs the icy North and is equated in the Tȟaté cycle with the giant Wazíya.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lakota_yanpa.name: govern the East, the place of dawn and new beginnings
lakota_yanpa.notes: Third-born of the Four Winds, Yaŋpá rules the eastern quarter of the dawn.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

lithuanian_saule.name: warm and quicken the earth as queen of the heavenly bodies
lithuanian_saule.notes: The sun goddess gives light and warmth and is mother of the planetary Daughters of the Sun; her weeping for a slain žaltys was said to bring drought.

sources.reference: Algirdas Julius Greimas, Of Gods and Men: Studies in Lithuanian Mythology

lithuanian_ausrine.name: kindle the fire and ready the horses for Saulė at daybreak
lithuanian_ausrine.notes: As a Daughter of the Sun and goddess of the Morning Star, Aušrinė lights the way of the dawn and prepares Saulė for her daily journey across the sky.

sources.reference: Algirdas Julius Greimas, Of Gods and Men: Studies in Lithuanian Mythology

lithuanian_velnias.name: master cattle, hidden wealth, magic, and craft
lithuanian_velnias.notes: The chthonic Velnias is lord of livestock and underground treasure and a cunning shape-shifter; he steals Perkūnas's cattle and water and hides them beneath stones and roots.

lakota_wi.name: Sun Dance
lakota_wi.notes: The supreme ceremony of the Lakota, danced around a sacred cottonwood pole hung with a buffalo skull; dancers fulfil vows by gazing at the sun and by piercing, offering their flesh for the renewal of the people and the world.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, The Sun Dance and Other Ceremonies of the Oglala Division of the Teton Dakota

lakota_wohpe.name: rites of the Sacred Calf Pipe
lakota_wohpe.notes: As White Buffalo Calf Woman she gave the Calf Pipe Bundle and the Seven Sacred Rites; the pipe is smoked in prayer to carry the people's words to Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka.

sources.reference: Joseph Epes Brown, The Sacred Pipe: Black Elk's Account of the Seven Rites of the Oglala Sioux

lithuanian_saule.name: midsummer solstice festival
lithuanian_saule.notes: Bonfires, circle dances, divination, wreaths, and the greeting of the rising sun mark the longest day; also called Joninės after Christianization.

sources.reference: Algirdas Julius Greimas, Of Gods and Men: Studies in Lithuanian Mythology

lithuanian_perkunas.name: goat sacrifice and oak rite
lithuanian_perkunas.cadence: in time of drought or need
lithuanian_perkunas.notes: Perkūnas was honoured at sacred oaks and with the sacrifice of a goat, as recorded for the Sudovian rite, to invoke rain and avert storms.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

lithuanian_gabija.name: offering and banking of the hearth-fire
lithuanian_gabija.notes: The first loaf of bread, with salt and water, was offered to the household fire; each evening the women banked the coals with ashes to 'put Gabija to bed' so the fire would not wander.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

lithuanian_zemyna.name: libation and kissing of the earth
lithuanian_zemyna.cadence: at sowing, harvest, and rites of passage
lithuanian_zemyna.notes: A libation of beer was poured on the ground with thanks; bread from the last harvest was buried and a black piglet might be sacrificed to begin the sowing, and the earth was kissed in greeting and farewell.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

lepcha_kongchen.name: Pang Lhabsol
lepcha_kongchen.notes: Kanchenjunga is honoured as guardian of the land with prayers, ritual dances, and offerings (the first of the millet-beer tongba is offered to the peak) to seek the mountain-deity's protection and blessing.

sources.reference: Halfdan Siiger, The Lepchas: Culture and Religion of a Himalayan People

lugbara_adro.name: riverside propitiation of the immanent god
lugbara_adro.notes: The dangerous earthly Adro is propitiated at shrines by rivers, large trees, and rocks; formerly with child sacrifice, since the 1930s with the sacrifice of a ram.

sources.reference: John Middleton, Lugbara Religion: Ritual and Authority among an East African People

attributes.name: great outstretched wings, often carved separately and attached
attributes.notes: Kwakwaka'wakw crest poles uniquely give the Thunderbird broad wings affixed to the figure; the face and claws are commonly painted yellow.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, The Social Organization and the Secret Societies of the Kwakiutl Indians

attributes.name: recurved feather-horns and powerful curved beak
attributes.notes: Distinguished from the eagle by curling appendages above the head and a strongly hooked beak.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, The Religion of the Kwakiutl Indians

attributes.name: a serpent head at each end with a central human face, all horned
attributes.notes: Rendered with protruding tongues and spiral or upturned snouts; painted on house-fronts, settees, masks, bows, and ceremonial belts.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, The Social Organization and the Secret Societies of the Kwakiutl Indians

attributes.name: the sun as a red disk, the chief of the sky
attributes.notes: Represented in the Sun Dance by the sacred pole and the painted circle, and addressed as the source of light and the cardinal virtues.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, The Sun Dance and Other Ceremonies of the Oglala Division of the Teton Dakota
James R. Walker, The Sun Dance and Other Ceremonies of the Oglala Division of the Teton Dakota

attributes.name: the blue of the sky, his proper color
attributes.notes: Blue is the color of Škáŋ; in the Sun Dance the sky is honoured with blue paint and offerings.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

attributes.name: rough rock and stone, hardened from his self-emptied body

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

attributes.name: the color red, his sacred color
attributes.notes: Red is Íŋyaŋ's color in the system of the four directions and the four Superior Gods.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

attributes.name: vast wings, a sharp beak, and talons, dwelling in a cloud-nest in the West
attributes.notes: Often unseen or shown as zigzag (forked) lightning lines; the heyókȟa paint and act out his contrary nature.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

sacredPlants.name: cedar / mountain juniper (burned for protection from lightning)

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

attributes.name: a vast horned serpent of the deep waters, scaled and armored
attributes.notes: Her petrified bones were identified with the fossil ridges of the Badlands; her shed power lay in her horn.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual

sacredAnimals.name: the white buffalo calf (her form on departing)

sources.reference: Joseph Epes Brown, The Sacred Pipe

attributes.name: one face of surpassing beauty and a second face of horror
attributes.notes: The Double-Face Woman shows only her fair side to lure, then turns to reveal the hideous second face given her by Škáŋ.

sources.reference: James R. Walker, Lakota Myth

attributes.name: the sun-wheel and rosette, and gilded shoes on a silver hill
attributes.notes: Geometric sun-signs (wheels, rosettes) carved on distaffs, shrines, and woven into cloth represent her eternal round.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

sacredAnimals.name: the žaltys (grass snake), her sacred household animal

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

attributes.name: a vigorous grey-bearded old man in white and black, hurling fire from the sky

sources.reference: Algirdas Julius Greimas, Of Gods and Men: Studies in Lithuanian Mythology
Marija Gimbutas, The Balts
Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

attributes.name: a figure clad in silver and grey, dwelling on a silver mountain
attributes.notes: In folklore he descends as an old wanderer in a grey coat to test human goodness; he bears a shining (silver or green) sword.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts
Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

attributes.name: a woman clothed in red, or a cat, stork, or rooster
attributes.notes: Gabija takes zoomorphic form moving through the house as the living fire.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

attributes.name: appears as a cuckoo calling from a linden, and as a spinner of the thread of life
attributes.notes: The number of the cuckoo's calls foretells the length of a life; she is also pictured as a swan or duck.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts
Marija Gimbutas, The Balts
Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

attributes.name: the eight-pointed morning star, herald of the dawn

sources.reference: Algirdas Julius Greimas, Of Gods and Men: Studies in Lithuanian Mythology

attributes.name: a one-eyed, clairvoyant shape-shifter, lord of the underworld
attributes.notes: His single eye marks his foresight (from IE *wel-, 'sight'); after Christianization his name passed to the Devil.

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

sacredAnimals.name: cattle and horses (the herds in his keeping)

sources.reference: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts

attributes.name: a very tall white man with only half a body — one eye, one arm, one leg
attributes.notes: The transcendent creator appears thus to the dying; carved half-figures stand at some shrines.

sources.reference: John Middleton, Lugbara Religion: Ritual and Authority among an East African People

attributes.name: little men and women, or water-serpents, haunting rivers, trees, and rocks
attributes.notes: They follow night travellers to guard them; to turn and look at one is to be killed.

sources.reference: John Middleton, Lugbara Religion: Ritual and Authority among an East African People
